explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. Jesus begins to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. This is a heavy moment, so I'll say it plain. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, and the two sons of Zebedee are right there to see it.

Rest is what the disciples end up doing, friend, but not Jesus. The text says He begins to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. That's about as far from calm as you can get. Keep that picture in your mind as the scene goes on.

Nothing in the passage says Jesus is angry with anyone, friend. What it says is that He begins to be sorrowful and deeply distressed. He also asks Peter, one of His disciples, and the two sons of Zebedee to stay with Him (Matthew 26:38). That's a man asking for company, so I think this is a sorrowful moment and not an angry one.

explanations.answer: Stay and keep watch with Him
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “Stay here and keep watch with Me.” It's a simple ask. He doesn't ask them to fix anything, only to stay and keep watch with Him. I think that says a lot about the moment.

explanations.answer: Go back and wake the others
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets sent to wake anybody, friend. The other disciples were told earlier, “Sit here while I go over there and pray.” What Jesus asks of these three is to stay and keep watch with Him. They aren't given a job to run off and do.

explanations.answer: Head into the city for help
explanations.explanation: No one is sent anywhere in this scene, baker. Jesus says, “Stay here and keep watch with Me.” The whole ask is about staying put. Going off for help isn't in the text at all.

I see why that sounds right, friend, because Jesus does pray, “…if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me.” But the prayer doesn't stop there. He goes on, “Yet not as I will, but as You will.” So His own will doesn't come first. The Father's will does.

Right, baker. Jesus does pray, “…if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me.” Then He finishes with, “Yet not as I will, but as You will.” His own will doesn't come first, and the Father's will does. That's what the text says.

That's it, friend. Jesus comes back and finds them sleeping. Before you judge them, ask yourself when you last stared down a heavy eyelid and lost. The text says in a moment that their eyes were heavy (Matthew 26:43).

The one praying in this scene is Jesus, baker. He goes off on His own and prays to His Father. When He comes back to the disciples, He finds them sleeping. They were asked to keep watch, and they're out cold.

Watching is exactly what Jesus asked them to do, friend. He said, “Stay here and keep watch with Me.” But when He returns, He finds them sleeping. His question to Peter, one of His disciples, is about that very thing: “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?”

explanations.answer: The spirit is willing but the body is weak
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Jesus says, “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” Anyone who has ever meant to get up early and then hit snooze knows exactly what that is. He speaks it plainly, and it's good to hear.

explanations.answer: The night is dark but the Father is near
explanations.explanation: That's a lovely sentence, friend, but it isn't what Jesus says here. His reason is, “For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” He gives it right after telling them to watch and pray. Stick close to His words, because they're the ones that count.

explanations.answer: The hour is late but the morning is coming
explanations.explanation: That one sounds poetic, baker, but it isn't in the text. Jesus gives this reason: “For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.” He says it right after, “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation.” His words are the ones to hold onto.
Not quite, friend. When Jesus comes back again, He finds them sleeping, and the text says it's because their eyes were heavy. They aren't awake and watching. Round two goes the same way as round one.
That's right, baker. Jesus returns and finds them sleeping again, “…for their eyes were heavy.” So He doesn't find them awake and watching. That's what the text says.
Yes, friend. Jesus goes away once more and prays a third time. His first prayer was in verse 39, the second time in verse 42, and now this one. Three trips away to pray, and the text keeps count.
That's right, baker. He prays a third time, “…saying the same thing.” The text gives no new words this time. His earlier prayer ended with “…may Your will be done.” (Matthew 26:42).

The count stops at three, friend. The text says Jesus went away “…once more and prayed a third time…” Before that came His first prayer and then a second time (Matthew 26:42). There's no fourth in this passage.
Jesus doesn't switch up His prayer, baker. The text says He prayed a third time, “…saying the same thing.” Nothing in the passage has Him saying the opposite. He says the same thing again.
That count runs way past the text, friend. Jesus prays a third time, and that's where the passage leaves it. Fifth isn't anywhere near the scene. Three prayers is all we see.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!” He tells them to get up first, and then He points out that the betrayer is coming. The scene is about to change fast.

The text says otherwise, friend. After Jesus returns from the third prayer, He tells the disciples, “Rise, let us go! See, My betrayer is approaching!” So He does tell them the betrayer is coming. And He says it before the betrayer even shows up.

explanations.answer: A large crowd with swords and clubs
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Judas, one of the Twelve, arrives “…accompanied by a large crowd armed with swords and clubs…” The text says they were sent from the chief priests and elders of the people. He didn't come alone.

explanations.answer: A group of shepherds with staffs
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention shepherds, friend. It says Judas, one of the Twelve, arrives with a large crowd armed with swords and clubs. That's the crowd the text describes. Staffs aren't on its list.

The text doesn't mention tax collectors, baker. Judas, one of the Twelve, comes with “…a large crowd armed with swords and clubs…” The text says they were sent from the chief priests and elders of the people. That's who is behind them.
Yes, friend. The crowd was “…sent from the chief priests and elders of the people.” The text tells us exactly who sent them. It's the leaders of Israel behind this.
The text says it plainly, baker. The crowd with Judas was “…sent from the chief priests and elders of the people.” So it's true that these leaders sent them. Judas isn't running this on his own.

You've got it, friend. Judas told the crowd, “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.” A kiss was the signal, and it had been arranged ahead of time. That's what the text says, and it's a heavy detail.
Pointing would've been a signal, baker, but it isn't the one in the text. Judas arranged this: “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.” The signal is a kiss. That's the detail to hold onto.
A bow isn't the signal in the text, friend. Judas told the crowd, “The One I kiss is the man; arrest Him.” He goes directly to Jesus, says “Greetings, Rabbi!” and kisses Him. The signal was the kiss.
That's what Jesus says, baker. “‘Friend,’ Jesus replied, ‘do what you came for.’” He answers Judas with that word right after the kiss. Then the men step forward and arrest Him.
Brother is a warm word, friend, but it isn't the one Jesus uses. He says, “Friend,” and then, “do what you came for.” That's His answer to Judas after the kiss. Stick to the word the text gives.
Jesus doesn't say neighbor here, baker. After the kiss He tells Judas, “Friend, do what you came for.” That's the word the text gives. Then the men seize Him.
Not quite, friend. One of Jesus' companions does try to fight back. He draws his sword and strikes the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. So somebody did swing.

That's right, baker. One of Jesus' companions draws his sword and strikes the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. So someone with Jesus does try to fight back. It happens right as the men seize Him.
That's what Jesus says, friend. He tells the companion, “Put your sword back in its place…” and then explains, “For all who draw the sword will die by the sword.” He answers him directly.
The text says otherwise, baker. Jesus tells the companion, “Put your sword back in its place…” He doesn't cheer him on, and He doesn't ignore it. He answers him directly.

explanations.answer: More than twelve legions of angels
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says the Father “…will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels?” A legion is a big group, and He says more than twelve of them. That's the help He says is one call away.
Twelve is in the verse, friend, but the soldiers aren't. Jesus says the Father will put at His disposal “…more than twelve legions of angels?” It's angels, and the Father would send them at once.
No Roman soldiers in this answer, baker. Jesus says His Father “…will at once put at My disposal more than twelve legions of angels?” So the help is angels. And it's more than twelve legions.

explanations.answer: Because Scripture says it must happen this way
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Jesus gives, friend. He asks, “But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?” He's the One who can call on the angels, and He doesn't. Later He adds, “But this has all happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled.” (Matthew 26:56)

explanations.answer: Because His Father told Him to stay quiet
explanations.explanation: The text never says His Father told Him to stay quiet, baker. The reason Jesus gives is, “But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?” We stay with the reason He actually says. No quiet order in the passage.

explanations.answer: Because the priests would set Him free later
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the passage says the priests would set Him free, friend. The reason Jesus gives is, “But how then would the Scriptures be fulfilled that say it must happen this way?” The chief priests and elders are the ones who sent the crowd (Matthew 26:47). That's all this passage says about them.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “Every day I sat teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me.” He points that out to the crowd. They came with swords and clubs, but He had been right there teaching in the open.

The text says otherwise, friend. Jesus tells the crowd, “Every day I sat teaching in the temple courts, and you did not arrest Me.” He reminds them of exactly that. So it's true that He was teaching every day and they hadn't arrested Him.
Yes, baker. The text says, “Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.” I think this one hurts, so I won't dress it up. It's right there in the passage, as the last line of the scene.

One of Jesus' companions did draw a sword earlier, friend, and Jesus told him to put it back. But the last line says all the disciples “…deserted Him and fled.” So defended isn't the word. I think this is one of the hard parts of the story.

Nobody is warning anyone at the end of this passage, baker. The text says, “Then all the disciples deserted Him and fled.” That's the whole ending of the scene. It's a heavy one, so I'll leave it plain.
